summary: Specifies a base profile for X.509 v3 certificates and v2 CRLs for use with the United States National Security Agency's Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite, applying to US National Security Systems. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A strict set of rules for digital ID cards used in certain US government systems, naming which math tools they may use.

questions: nsa commercial national security algorithm suite
subtitle: Cryptographic requirements for digital certificates in US government systems.

tldr.problem: US National Security Systems need strict, standardized rules for how X.509 digital certificates and revocation lists are structured to ensure interoperability and security. Different implementations might use weak cryptography or incompatible formats.
tldr.mechanism: This profile specifies mandatory algorithms, key sizes, and certificate extensions for use with the National Security Agency's Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite. It requires either ECDSA with the P-384 elliptic curve or RSA with 3072 or 4096-bit keys, always using SHA-384 hashing.
tldr.outcome: Certificates and systems conforming to this profile are assured to use cryptography judged secure for US National Security Systems. The standardized profile enables interoperability while preventing weak or unsafe choices.

facts.label: Allowed key types
facts.value: ECDSA P-384, ECDH P-384, RSA-3072, RSA-4096

facts.label: Applicability
facts.value: US National Security Systems and US Government high-value systems

today: RFC 8603 is an Informational RFC published in May 2019 and is not obsoleted. It provides the current CNSA Suite certificate profile for US National Security Systems. This represents the NSA's cryptographic guidance as of 2019, with expectations of future transitions to quantum-resistant algorithms.

sections.title: The CNSA Suite and Its Purpose
sections.content:
The United States National Security Agency publishes guidance on cryptographic algorithms for use in government systems. This RFC specifies a base profile for X.509 v3 Certificates and Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) for the Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite. The profile applies to US National Security Systems as described in NIST Special Publication 800-59, but is also appropriate for any other US Government system processing high-value information.

The CNSA Suite was established to provide near-term flexibility in transitioning cryptography while anticipating the future arrival of quantum-resistant algorithms. Rather than define new algorithms, RFC 8603 profiles the use of commercial algorithms in a restricted, secure manner. The profile builds on RFC 5280 (the standard X.509 certificate specification) and elevates some optional requirements to mandatory levels.
sections.plainLanguage: The NSA has picked certain math methods that are secure enough for government secrets. This RFC says how to build ID cards using only those methods, so everyone does it the same secure way.

sections.title: The Allowed Algorithms
sections.content:
Every CNSA Suite certificate MUST contain exactly one of the following:

ECDSA with P-384: Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm using the P-384 curve for signature keys, or Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) also using P-384 for key establishment.

RSA with 3072 or 4096 bits: RSA keys for either signatures or key transport.

All signatures must use SHA-384 hashing, regardless of which key type is used. For RSA, the signature method MUST be RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 (PKCS #1 version 1.5).

The profile does not prohibit RSA-PSS signatures in protocols, but Certification Authorities conforming to this profile will not issue certificates specifying RSA-PSS for subject public keys. If protocols use RSA-PSS, they MUST use SHA-384, mask generation function 1, and a 48-octet salt length.
sections.plainLanguage: Use either a fancy curve-based method (P-384) or really large number-based method (RSA with huge keys). Either way, always hash with SHA-384.

sections.title: Certificate Structure and Extensions
sections.content:
Certificates must be version 3 (set to value 2 in the version field). For the public key information, ECDSA/ECDH certificates MUST use the algorithm ID id-ecPublicKey with secp384r1 as the named curve. RSA certificates MUST use rsaEncryption with NULL parameters.

Different types of certificates require different extensions. Self-signed CA certificates MUST include subjectKeyIdentifier, keyUsage (marked critical, with keyCertSign and cRLSign bits set), and basicConstraints (marked critical, with cA set to true).

Non-self-signed CA certificates MUST include authorityKeyIdentifier, keyUsage (critical, with keyCertSign and cRLSign bits), and basicConstraints (critical, with cA true). If certificate policy is asserted, certificatePolicies MUST be included (non-critical).

End-entity certificates MUST include authorityKeyIdentifier and keyUsage (critical). For signature certificates, digitalSignature bit MUST be set. For key establishment certificates (ECDH or RSA), keyAgreement or keyEncipherment bits MUST be set.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate is like an ID card with a photo, name, and various stamps. Different types of ID cards need different stamps. The profile says which stamps are required for each type.

sections.title: CRL Requirements and Interoperability
sections.content:
Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs), which announce revoked certificates, MUST follow the same signature and algorithm requirements as certificates themselves. The signatures on CRLs MUST use the same rules specified in the certificate section: ECDSA with P-384 and SHA-384, or RSA with 3072/4096 bits and SHA-384.

RFC 8603 also specifies that implementations MUST be able to process both compressed and uncompressed forms of elliptic curve points, though all implementations MUST accept the uncompressed form. The RSA exponent e MUST satisfy 2^16 < e < 2^256 and be odd.

The profile is a base profile. Specific communities (such as those managing National Security Systems) may define community-specific profiles that further restrict contents, add optional extensions, or mandate extensions not required in this base profile. However, communications between distinct communities MUST conform with the base profile for interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules apply to the lists of revoked IDs, too. And different groups can add stricter rules if they need to, but everyone must at least follow this basic recipe to talk to each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Limitations
sections.content:
A single key pair SHOULD NOT be used for both signatures and key establishment per NIST Special Publication 800-57. This separates the risk: a compromised signature key does not compromise key establishment, and vice versa.

The RFC does not define new cryptographic algorithms, nor does it prove their security. It references existing standards: FIPS 186 for DSA and ECDSA, RFC 5280 for X.509, and NIST publications for key management. Implementations are assumed to follow standard cryptographic practices.

The profile applies to US National Security Systems and other high-value government systems. It is made publicly available for use by developers and operators of any system that requires this level of cryptographic assurance, though classified systems and their implementation details remain outside the scope of this public RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Use different keys for signing and encrypting. Don't try to create your own math—follow the published standards. This is for serious government security, not everyday websites.
